title: Economic Bulletin Issue 2, 2026 - European Central Bank
summary: At its March 19, 2026 meeting, the ECB Governing Council kept interest rates unchanged, citing heightened uncertainty from the Middle East war that creates upside inflation risks and downside growth risks. ECB staff raised headline inflation projections to 2.6% for 2026 (from December 2025 forecast) while cutting GDP growth forecasts to 0.9% for 2026, reflecting disruption to commodity markets and weakened confidence.
key_points: ECB Governing Council kept the three key interest rates unchanged at the March 19, 2026 meeting
Headline inflation projected at 2.6% in 2026, 2.0% in 2027, and 2.1% in 2028, revised up from December 2025 projections due to higher energy prices from the Middle East war
GDP growth projected at 0.9% in 2026, 1.3% in 2027, and 1.4% in 2028, down 0.3 percentage points for 2026 and 0.1 for 2027 from prior projections
February 2026 HICP inflation was 1.9%, up from 1.7% in January; inflation excluding energy and food rose to 2.4%
War in the Middle East is disrupting commodity markets, weighing on real incomes and confidence, with supply disruptions potentially pushing inflation above baseline and growth below
ECB reiterated it is not pre-committing to a particular rate path and will follow a data-dependent, meeting-by-meeting approach
why_it_matters: The ECB's decision to hold rates while simultaneously revising up inflation and revising down growth signals a delicate balancing act amid geopolitical uncertainty. Markets should note that the ECB has explicitly acknowledged the Middle East war as a material risk to both price stability and economic growth, increasing the likelihood of policy divergence depending on how the situation evolves.
macro_context: The ECB notes euro area Q4 2025 GDP grew 0.2% driven by domestic demand, with unemployment near historical lows and solid private sector balance sheets. However, the March projections incorporate war-related uncertainty, with staff analysis suggesting a prolonged energy supply disruption would push inflation higher and growth lower than baseline. The Governing Council emphasized that fiscal responses to energy shocks should be temporary, targeted, and tailored.
